title: Few-shot Prompting
subtitle: Topic: Few-shot Prompting · Subject: Prompt Engineering · 3 beginner, 2 medium and 2 advanced questions with seven original instructional SVG diagrams and a runnable Python prompt-construction example.
hero:
FEW-SHOT PROMPTING · VISUAL STUDY

Teach the task through a small set of examples.

Discover why in-context demonstrations help define a task, how to select and order them, and how to test improvements without weight updates or evaluation leakage.

Illustrative labels and examples. No live model is called in the Python demonstration.

questions.stem: What is Few-shot Prompting in large language models, and how does learning from examples placed in the prompt differ from fine-tuning model weights?
options: Few-shot prompting places labeled examples in the prompt and updates selected model weights before the new question. Those parameter changes persist across requests, allowing the model to retain task-specific learning.
Few-shot prompting gives a model a small set of labeled input–output examples before a new task. It uses these examples during inference without changing its trained weights.

Few-shot prompting uses a few training examples to compute task-specific gradients in the background. Those learned updates remain available after the prompt ends, unlike ordinary instruction following.

Few-shot prompting presents several sample outputs and treats them as replacement training labels for the new request. It requires rewriting the model's stored vocabulary probabilities before the next prediction.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Few-shot prompting supplies a few input–output examples inside the text sent to a model. The model uses these demonstrations as context to handle a new input; unlike fine-tuning, it does not update its parameters with gradients. For a school office, a prompt might show that an exam-fee question belongs to Billing and a login issue belongs to Account, then request the category for another message. The examples guide the response at inference time.

questions.stem: How do zero-shot, one-shot and few-shot prompting differ, and what parts of a prompt show the model which outputs and labels are expected?
options: Zero-shot prompts contain a task instruction and no examples; one-shot prompts contain one example; few-shot prompts contain several examples. The difference is mainly whether the outputs include explicit reasoning explanations.

Zero-shot prompting asks for a label without examples, one-shot includes one input–output sample, and few-shot includes several. Examples become effective only after a task-specific gradient training step.

Zero-shot gives no demonstrations, one-shot gives a single demonstration, and few-shot gives several. The new task should appear before the examples so the model can retroactively compare earlier output labels.
Zero-shot supplies no examples, one-shot supplies one, and few-shot supplies several input–output demonstrations. Label names, separators and an unlabeled new input define the pattern to continue.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Zero-shot prompting gives the task without demonstrations. One-shot provides a single example, and few-shot provides a small number of examples showing the desired input–output pattern. The task instruction, label names, separators and final unlabeled case clarify what to produce. For restaurant-review sentiment, a few-shot prompt might demonstrate Positive, Negative and Neutral reviews before asking for the label of a new comment. More examples do not automatically produce better results.

QUESTION 02 · VISUAL LESSON

Count the examples supplied to the model, not the number of output tokens or training epochs.

questions.stem: How should Few-shot Prompting examples be selected and formatted to cover relevant categories, reduce ambiguity and support reliable classification of new inputs?
options: Choose representative examples from the allowed categories, verify their input–output pairs, and keep separators and labels consistent. Include meaningful edge cases when they are relevant to the new task.

Choose examples from the most frequent category and repeat that label consistently. The model can infer the other categories from their names, so class coverage is unnecessary for few-shot classification.
Choose examples with different categories but assign the longest examples to the same class. This makes the pattern easier to notice, because the model can rely on length instead of input meaning.

Choose samples that share exact phrases with the final benchmark questions, then include the correct benchmark labels. This reduces ambiguity and gives a more accurate estimate on unseen evaluation examples.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Few-shot examples should represent the task's real inputs and allowed outputs. Check that the labels are appropriate and the format is consistent; include examples of important categories and boundaries when useful. For industrial status messages, one example each of ERROR, WARNING and NORMAL can clarify the target labels. Avoid demonstrations that merely match superficial wording or contain test-set answers. Research also shows that format, label space and input distribution can influence in-context performance, so validate example choices rather than assuming one recipe always wins.

QUESTION 03 · VISUAL LESSON

Coverage and clear formatting help learners; actual model sensitivity should be tested.

questions.stem: Why can the order, balance and wording of Few-shot Prompting demonstrations change a model's answer, and how can this sensitivity be evaluated fairly?
options: Demonstration order can affect predictions, so always put the most common label last and judge the prompt using its strongest observed final-test score. That produces an unbiased estimate of deployment quality.

Example order matters only when the prompt includes contradictory instructions, while class imbalance is harmless if label names are explicit. Testing one order is sufficient for reliable few-shot evaluation.

Large language models may react differently to demonstration order, class balance or wording. Try several well-formed variants on development data and reserve the final test set for unbiased evaluation.

Changing order changes the available label set and therefore invalidates the few-shot task itself. Instead of reordering demonstrations, compare only prompts with entirely different allowed output categories.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Few-shot predictions can be sensitive to which examples appear, how labels are balanced and the order of demonstrations. Models may overuse a recent label or react to superficial phrasing. Test several candidate orders on a development set, report variability, and leave final test data untouched. For hotel-review categorization, placing several Negative reviews at the end might affect borderline predictions. This is a possible tendency, not a fixed rule, so it must be measured.

questions.stem: How can Python construct a Few-shot Prompting template from labeled examples, verify label coverage and format, and distinguish that check from actually running an LLM?
options: Build labeled prompt examples, then treat the target's expected label as the LLM's predicted label. Verifying the expected output within Python is enough to demonstrate the model would follow the examples.

Format each approved input–label example consistently, append a new unlabeled case, and check category coverage and prompt structure. Such assertions test construction but do not measure LLM accuracy.

Write few-shot demonstrations and append the target input, then count the prompt's characters as an estimate of classification accuracy. If all categories appear, the model's output is guaranteed to be valid.

Construct examples using labels inferred from the new test item and append those labels to the prompt. This tests the model fairly because the few-shot demonstrations are selected from the evaluation cases.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Use Python to store labeled examples, check their labels against an allowed set, format them consistently and append the new request with its answer slot blank. Assertions can verify the example count, label coverage and correct prompt ending. They do not tell us what an LLM would predict. In the runnable customer-support example, Billing, Technical and Account are demonstrated before a new duplicate-invoice ticket. Its known reference category is Billing, but no LLM is called.
questions.figure:
QUESTION 05 · VISUAL LESSON
Python · 17 runnable lines · prompt construction only (no model API)
examples = [
    ('Please reverse a double charge.', 'Billing'),
    ('The app freezes at startup.', 'Technical'),
    ('I cannot reset my password.', 'Account'),
]
allowed = {'Billing', 'Technical', 'Account'}
def demonstration(text, label):
    assert label in allowed
    return f'Ticket: {text}\nCategory: {label}'
instructions = 'Classify a support ticket as Billing, Technical, or Account.\n'
prompt = instructions + '\n\n'.join(demonstration(*item) for item in examples)
prompt += '\n\nTicket: My invoice has a duplicate charge.\nCategory:'
expected_label = 'Billing'  # independent known example label
assert len(examples) == 3 and {label for _, label in examples} == allowed
assert prompt.endswith('Category:') and expected_label in allowed
print('Examples:', len(examples), '| All categories represented:', True)
print('Expected label (not model-generated):', expected_label)

The Python panel builds and checks a prompt; it cannot estimate model performance without a model.

questions.stem: How can retrieval-based example selection and context-window limits affect Few-shot Prompting quality, token cost and robustness on a changing workload?
options: Select all available demonstrations, even when they crowd out the latest user request. More labeled examples always improve performance and reduce output latency because they provide additional context.
Retrieve only the single most semantically similar example to each new request, even if this removes all other categories. A matching phrase alone guarantees correct few-shot classification.
Keep a fixed set of examples regardless of changing input types, because dynamic selection would update model parameters. Context-window limits matter only when a fine-tuning job is running.
Choose relevant, varied examples that fit the context budget while reserving space for instructions, input and output. Evaluate accuracy, token cost, latency and example-selection stability.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Few-shot prompts consume context tokens, so very long or poorly selected demonstrations may increase cost, slow requests or crowd out important instructions. Retrieval can select examples similar to the new task, but diversity and correct label coverage still matter. Budget space for instructions, examples, the new request and the answer. For a travel-help chatbot, dynamically selected booking and cancellation examples may help more than unrelated hotel questions. Compare answer quality and latency rather than assuming more examples are better.

questions.stem: How should Few-shot Prompting be evaluated and deployed responsibly while preventing evaluation leakage, sensitive-example exposure and misleading claims of generalization?
options: Compare prompt variants on identical held-out cases, tuning examples only on development data. Exclude private records and report accuracy, token cost, order sensitivity and uncertainty.

Choose demonstrations from final test questions because their correct labels best represent the evaluation target. Then compare prompt variants on those same tests to measure realistic performance without contamination.

Publish only the best few-shot score across prompt orders and evaluation seeds, omitting example selection details. The selected result is unbiased so long as the underlying model weights remain fixed.

Use real customer conversations in public prompt templates to capture authentic language, even if identifiers remain visible. Few-shot prompting is safe because demonstrations do not permanently update model weights.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Evaluate prompt styles on the same held-out cases using consistent metrics. Select examples and tune order on development data, not final-test answers. Record prompt versions, sample counts, tokens, latency and variation across runs. Protect personal data and assess whether demonstrations include sensitive or copyrighted material. For a municipal complaint-routing system, anonymized training examples can guide prompts without exposing citizens' addresses or allowing test-case labels into the prompt. Few-shot prompting may help, but deployment gains require measurement.
